messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Michael, a 54‑year‑old forester in a small Midwestern town, recalled the day that would forever change his life with a clarity that bordered on pain. It was early spring, and he was alone on a logging road cutting through a dense pine stand when a chainsaw‑laden skidder rolled out of control. The heavy steel frame of the skidder slid across the gravel, slamming into a fellow worker’s back and leaving the man with a shattered vertebra. Michael’s hands, still slick with oil, had barely released the chainsaw handle when the engine sputtered, and in that split second the machine’s wheels struck a loose rock, sending the skidder careening. The victim’s scream rang out, and Michael’s heart dropped to his gut. Even years later, the memory of that violent collision triggers a burning ache in his left shoulder, a somatic echo that tells him he still carries the weight of the accident. That ache becomes a portal to a broader sense of threat. Whenever he feels the pressure of muscle pain, his mind instantly zooms to the scene of the injury, and he cannot relax even in the safety of his own home. The painful sensation signals danger, and his mind interprets it as a reminder that something catastrophic could happen again. At work, walking past a group of coworkers, he watches them intently for the slightest change in posture or pace, convinced that a misplaced step could trigger a new disaster. Strangers approaching on the forest path—truck drivers, delivery riders, even a casual jogger—instantly set off alarms; their unfamiliarity feels like a potential threat even when they pose no real danger. Each of these triggers feeds into his hypervigilant state, leaving him exhausted and on edge. The same triggers also bring back vivid memories. The pain in his shoulder conjures a bodily reenactment: his arms locked in the same position he had held on the skidder, his breath shallow and ragged. When he recalls the victim’s pain and the roar of the chainsaw, a wave of rage surges through him, as if the memory is an active threat. Alongside the fury, an overwhelming grief crashes in, and Michael feels as though he has lost his sense of self. These memories in turn deepen his negative appraisals. He comes to believe that there is something inherently flawed about him; he sees the accident as a testament to his own intrinsic fault. The memory of being unable to control the chainsaw fuels the conviction that he can no longer rely on himself, and the haunting realization that he is no longer capable of the precise work that had defined his career. Each recollection reinforces the idea that the event was his fault, and this belief keeps him trapped in a loop of self‑blame and distress. In turn, the heightened sense of threat feeds back into his memories. Even when he is not in pain, the mere sight of a heavy piece of equipment or the sound of an engine can trigger the same bodily reenactment, as if his body has learned to anticipate danger from any cue associated with his trauma. This anticipatory threat keeps his mind from fully relaxing, ensuring that his memories stay vivid and immediate. The persistent threat also magnifies his negative appraisals, as he watches himself fail to maintain control and concludes that he is still defective. The cycle between triggers, threat, memory, and negative appraisal tightens, and each time it spins he feels more isolated, more exhausted, and increasingly convinced that he cannot function in the forest as he once did. Over months, Michael began to avoid certain jobs: he no longer accepted assignments that required operating large machinery or moving through dense brush alone. The avoidance, though rational on the surface, left him unemployed for weeks, and the loss of routine made him feel more powerless. His wife, Sarah, noticed the change; she saw him pacing the kitchen at night, eyes darting to the back door whenever someone passed. She tried to reassure him that no one was coming, but Michael’s gaze kept searching for danger. Their conversations grew strained, and Michael began to fear that his inability to relax would ruin their marriage. The culmination of this spiraling distress, coupled with a recent incident in which he slipped on a wet log and nearly fell into a ravine, pushed him to finally seek help. He is now most afraid that his thoughts will continue to spiral out of control and that he will lose his sense of safety and identity, yet he also hopes that therapy will teach him to stop seeing every rustle of leaves or every distant truck as a prelude to disaster.
